title: System Design, Data Structures & High Scalability Architecture
description: Fundamental concepts in large-scale system architecture, high-throughput distributed systems, algorithms, and technical interview problem solving.
detailedExplanation: Designing scalable enterprise applications requires balancing availability vs consistency (CAP Theorem), implementing caching tiers (Redis), database read replicas / sharding, message queues (Kafka, RabbitMQ) for asynchronous processing, and choosing optimal data structures (HashMaps, Trees, Graphs, Heaps) for sub-millisecond execution.
architectureFlow: Client -> Global CDN -> Load Balancer (Nginx/ALB) -> API Gateway -> Stateless Microservices -> Redis Cache -> Primary DB (Writes) + Read Replicas (Reads)
examples: Rate Limiter implementation (Token Bucket / Sliding Window Log)
Distributed Chat / Messaging System design (Slack / WhatsApp)

interviewQuestions.question: Explain the CAP Theorem in Distributed Systems.
interviewQuestions.answer: CAP states that a distributed system can guarantee at most 2 of 3 properties simultaneously: Consistency (all nodes see same data), Availability (every request receives non-error response), and Partition Tolerance (system operates despite network breaks). Virtually all cloud systems pick CP or AP.

interviewQuestions.question: How does a Sliding Window Rate Limiter work?
interviewQuestions.answer: It tracks request timestamps in a sorted set (or Redis zset). When a new request arrives, old timestamps outside the current window are removed, and if remaining count < limit, request is allowed.

bestPractices: Design stateless API servers so horizontal autoscaling is trivial
Decouple heavy synchronous tasks into async message queues (Kafka / BullMQ)
Always design with failure in mind — implement circuit breakers and retries with exponential backoff
commonMistakes: Single Point of Failure (SPOF) without failover database replicas
Premature optimization before identifying actual bottleneck via profiling
